about.introduction: I am a Computer System Technology student exploring how software can make complex systems interactive—from folding paper to querying data and navigating branching chess timelines.
story: My projects often start with curiosity about a field I have not worked in before. Implementing a paper-folding solver introduced me to finite element methods; building a browser database workspace let me explore interpreter-adjacent work.

I use existing tools and research as foundations, then focus on the parts I want to understand and build. Small experiments, existing tests, and realistic scope help me turn those ideas into working demos.
about.careerGoal: I am looking for a junior development role where I can contribute code, API integrations, tests, and documentation while learning through code review.

projects.name: Origami Lab
projects.description: Explore 25 paper studies in 3D, adjust their folds, and inspect how a flat sheet becomes a structure.

image.alt: Origami Lab displaying a blue Miura tessellation at 65% fold with the pattern collection and paper controls

roleAndChallenge.text: I implemented a paper-folding solver from a published finite element method. The numerical method came from research; translating it into a working solver was my contribution, and FEM was new to me.

Before tackling the full origami problem, I used AI to build small numerical experiments to check my implementation. Roughly 30% of my test cases converged on my laptop but failed on my phone. Reading the documentation led me to a loss of precision in FP16 storage. Correcting that issue resolved the affected cases.

reflection.label: Takeaway
reflection.text: This project taught me to validate unfamiliar mathematics in small steps and to investigate numerical storage when the same implementation behaves differently across devices.

reflection.label: In the demo
reflection.text: Captured from the live app, the screenshot shows a Miura pattern at 65% fold. Adjust folds and inspect crease geometry in the demo to explore the solver’s interactive output.

projects.name: SQL/REPL
projects.description: Query CSV, Parquet, and JSON with DuckDB in the browser, explore results, and build charts without a backend.

image.alt: SQL/REPL dark editor with highlighted analytics SQL and twelve query result rows

roleAndChallenge.text: I wanted to explore work adjacent to compilers and interpreters within a limited timeframe. I built the UI and a changeset algorithm for a miniature in-browser database, building on an existing codebase rather than writing the SQL engine.

To prioritize compute and query efficiency, the algorithm computes differences against the original database snapshot instead of computing an update every time. My implementation passed the original codebase’s insert, edit, and deletion tests.

reflection.label: Takeaway
reflection.text: The project gave me experience designing state changes around a clear baseline and checking behavior against existing tests. Efficiency drove the design; I have not established a measured speedup.

reflection.label: In the demo
reflection.text: The live workspace demonstrates the editor and browser-based querying. Its screenshot uses an AI-assisted sample analytics query to show syntax highlighting and tabular results.

projects.name: 5D Chess · AI Spectator
projects.description: Explore chess across branching timelines, navigate alternate game continuations, and configure AI players.

image.alt: 5D Chess in its dark theme showing the two initial boards

roleAndChallenge.text: Discovering that 5D chess with time travel was a real game, and remembering AlphaGo, made me curious about letting AI play it. I adapted an open-source game and rewrote its interface to supply game state to AI players instead of human players.

Because the models were not specifically trained for this game, I supplied its rules and current state, with retrieval support limited to two queries per turn, each under 50 ms. I observed time travel and timeline branching in roughly 80% of my test cases. Token costs limited the number of completed games.

reflection.label: Takeaway
reflection.text: The experiment made inference cost a practical constraint on testing. Exercising unusual game mechanics is a useful result, but it does not establish strong play or reliable completion of full matches.

reflection.label: In the demo
reflection.text: The screenshot captures the initial boards. Open the demo to explore AI configuration, navigate game continuations, and inspect branching timelines.

projects.name: Molecular Explorer
projects.description: Explore biological molecules in an interactive 3D viewer, from hemoglobin and DNA to proteins and RNA.

image.alt: Molecular Explorer showing a three-dimensional molecular structure alongside its molecule selection menu

roleAndChallenge.text: I initially wanted to create a visual library of organic chemistry reactions. In the sources I explored, structural-formula images were common, but conveniently usable spatial data was not. Collecting that data at the intended scale was unrealistic.

I narrowed the project to displaying existing protein structures. This was a scope and data-feasibility decision: the resulting Mol*-based viewer displays molecular structures; it does not simulate protein folding or chemical reactions.

reflection.label: Takeaway
reflection.text: Investigating the available data changed what I could reasonably deliver. Narrowing the idea preserved its visual exploration goal while avoiding an open-ended data collection effort.

reflection.label: In the demo
reflection.text: The screenshot captures a loaded structure in the live viewer. Select examples, rotate and zoom, or import molecular files to explore the revised project’s focus on existing structures.

projects.name: Internet Pulse
projects.description: Explore internet latency and reachability measurements across an interactive globe and world map.

image.alt: Internet Pulse globe displaying simulated network measurements and latency statistics

roleAndChallenge.text: I made Internet Pulse as an exploration of data visualization, an area I had not worked in before.
The project presents network measurements through a globe and world map, with filters for probe region and latency. Its scope is a focused visualization experiment.

reflection.label: Takeaway
reflection.text: The view needs context: arcs connect measurement endpoints rather than physical cable routes, and live coverage depends on available probes.

reflection.label: In the demo
reflection.text: The screenshot was captured from the live app in simulation mode. Use the demo to switch views and inspect measurements; the image illustrates the interface rather than current internet conditions.

technicalEvidence.title: Numerical implementation · Origami Lab
technicalEvidence.text: A research-derived FEM solver, checked with small numerical experiments and investigated across desktop and mobile. The case study explains the precision failure; the demo shows folding behavior.

technicalEvidence.title: Database state & UI · SQL/REPL
technicalEvidence.text: A browser workspace and snapshot-based changeset algorithm. The case study records passing existing insert, edit, and deletion tests; the demo shows the query interface.

softEvidence.title: Debugging across devices
paragraphs: FEM was unfamiliar territory, so I used AI-assisted numerical experiments to build confidence before applying my implementation to a large origami problem.
About 30% of my test cases converged on my laptop but failed on my phone. I investigated the documentation and traced the discrepancy to FP16 storage precision. Correcting it resolved those failures.

The lesson I take from this is to test assumptions at a small scale and consider device-dependent numerical behavior. This record summarizes my observations; the live folding demo is the accompanying artifact.

softEvidence.title: Choosing a feasible scope
paragraphs: My original goal was a visual library of organic chemistry reactions. The sources I found usually offered structural-formula images, not spatial data that could be conveniently used in a viewer.

Rather than undertake an unrealistic data-gathering effort, I changed the goal to displaying existing protein structures. The delivered viewer retains the visual exploration idea within a feasible scope.
This decision taught me to assess the data requirements before committing to the full feature set. The molecular viewer is evidence of the revised outcome, not a reaction or folding simulator.
